title: Kara and kangha, daily

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kirpan and the law: a promise and a rule meeting at a security line. Your line was faith and law. What did you find out about the rule where you live? Day one thousand two hundred ninety.

A string tied around a finger. A sticky note on the fridge. An alarm with a label on it. People lean on small things to hold big intentions, because big intentions slip away by lunchtime. Watch a Sikh at a kitchen counter, reaching for a knife to cut vegetables, and you might catch the light on a plain steel band at the wrist. Watch the same person at the end of the day, and you might see a small comb tucked into the knot of hair. Two of the five Ks are small enough to forget you're wearing them. Sikhs wear them precisely so they won't forget.
screen: `A STRING AROUND A FINGER.` → `A STEEL BAND AT THE WRIST.` → `SMALL ENOUGH TO FORGET.`

segments.voice: Start with the kara. It is a plain bracelet, usually of steel or iron, worn on the wrist by Sikhs who keep the five Ks, and by other Sikhs too. It isn't jewelry. No gold, no gems, no clasp. Sikhs often point to two things about it. First, its shape: a circle, with no beginning and no end, which they take as a reminder of the One without beginning or end. Second, its place: it sits on the wrist, right where the hand begins. Before the hand does anything, it passes the kara. So a Sikh reaching to take, to strike, to sign, to give, has a small steel question resting on the way: is this an act the Guru would stand behind? Now the kangha. We met it a few days ago as a tool of care, combing the uncut hair. Today look at it as a reminder. It lives in the hair all day, a quiet sign that a Sikh life is meant to be kept in order, clean and tended, not tangled and neglected. Some Sikhs combine the two in their own way: a touch of the kara before work, a moment with the kangha at night. Neither is magic. The code rejects charms and lucky objects, as we heard earlier on this path. The kara and the kangha don't protect anyone by themselves. They work only when they are noticed. That's why they're worn every day. A reminder you see once a year is a decoration. A reminder on your wrist all day is a practice. Touch and remember.
screen: `THE KARA: PLAIN STEEL, NO END.` · `IT SITS WHERE THE HAND BEGINS.` · `THE KANGHA: A LIFE KEPT IN ORDER.` · `NOT A CHARM: A REMINDER.` · then, large: `TOUCH AND REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: touch your wrist before acting. Settle, and breathe. Rest the fingers of one hand on the other wrist. If you wear a kara, feel the cool steel. If you don't, feel your pulse, or just the bone. Now picture the next thing your hands will do after the bell: pick up a phone, open a door, type a message, hold someone. Before that act, ask quietly: is this something I'd stand behind? Stay with your fingers on your wrist until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Kara and kangha. The steel bracelet at the wrist and the small comb in the hair: two of the five Ks, worn every day as reminders. Today's word.
Your line: touch and remember. Today, before one important act, touch your wrist, and ask whether it's something you'd stand behind. Day one thousand two hundred ninety.
